newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Telekom sale may boost Bonn EMU bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Telekom sale may boost Bonn EMU bid.

text.p: Germany's drive to qualify for the single European currency got a possible boost on Thursday with an agreement allowing the government to raise badly-needed cash by selling a stake in Deutsche Telekom AG.

The telecoms giant said it had agreed with the government that Bonn would transfer shares equivalent to 25 percent of Telekom's capital to the state development agency Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau (KfW).
The shares would be transferred in two steps in 1997 and 1998 and would be sold later to strategic investors.

Bonn is desperately seeking cash to cut its budget deficit to the equivalent of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), a target would-be members of the single European currency are supposed to meet this year to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

Embattled Finance Minister Theo Waigel had to compromise earlier this month with the Bundesbank over a plan to revalue central bank reserves. Thursday's deal marks another retreat by Waigel, who has had to promise that the Telekom shares will not be sold on the market before 2000.
This protects Telekom's 1.9 million shareholders, who bought shares when the group was partially privatised last year, from a sudden dilution of their investment.

But the sale could also cut Bonn's remaining 74 percent stake to less than a majority, freeing Telekom from state control earlier than planned. "Now new partnerships are possible that will considerably strengthen Telekom's position on the world market," chairman Ron Sommer told the company's first shareholders' meeting.

German government sources have said the sale could raise as much as 25 billion marks ($14.5 billion) over two years, but it is unclear whether Bonn will be able to use the funds to meet the budget targets for monetary union.
Telekom shares closed down nearly one percent on Thursday at 42.50 marks in a slightly higher broader market.
Germany is not the only country hoping that a sale of telecom shares could help to meet the EMU budget target.

In Paris a French government source said that new Socialist Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn was not against a partial sale of France Telecom, although no decision had been taken yet on the controversial issue.
The previous centre-right government decided to privatise France Telecom but earlier this month it lost power to a Socialist-led administration, which put the float on ice.

The Socialists have been hostile to privatisation but economists say revenue from France Telecom is urgently needed to shore up balance sheets of ailing state-owned companies without worsening the public deficit in the qualifying year for EMU.

Until the agreement over the Deutsche Telekom share sale, Waigel had left open the option of selling Telekom shares straight to the market. This would have raised considerably more cash for Bonn, but would probably have depressed the share price.

Under the deal Telekom will be able to work with the KfW to find strategic investors which could help its international expansion. "We are looking at current and future partners in the international telecommunications business," Sommer said, declining to mention any names.
Analysts say an equity swap between Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom is possible to anchor their strategic alliance, but only if France Telecom is privatised.

The two firms own 20 percent of U.S. long-distance carrier Sprint Corp and all three operate the Global One alliance. Deutsche Telekom has talked to Cable and Wireless Plc about a link between the British-based telecoms group and Global One, and it has sought a strategic partner in Asia.
Despite Bonn's plan to sell its shares, Sommer said Telekom would keep open its option of another capital increase of 287 million shares before the year 2000.
Sommer, addressing about 10,000 shareholders at its first annual meeting since going public, said the company was well placed as the German market raced towards full competition in January.

"But we will still have to give up market share," he said. "That's obvious and is a development that every former monopolist has to face. But we are prepared to offset lost market share with volume growth and higher sales."
Sommer also said Telekom had signed a preliminary interconnection agreement with Viag Interkom GmbH that it expects to finalise before the end of the year.
The deal with the joint venture of Viag and British Telecom ensures that Viag Interkom will be able to use Telekom's infrastructure to gain access to customers in local networks from January 1, 1998.
($ = 1.725 German Marks)
